source_text: Ταῦτα (Valesius emendat ταύτῃ) καὶ ὑμεῖς διὰ τῆς τοσαύτης νουθεσίας, τὴν ἀπὸ Πέτρου καὶ Παύλου φυτείαν γενηθεῖσαν Ῥωμαίων τε καὶ Κορινθίων συνεκεράσατε. καὶ γὰρ ἄμφω καὶ εἰς τὴν ἡμετέραν Κόρινθον φυτεύσαντες ἡμᾶς, ὁμοίως ἐδίδαξαν. ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ εἰς τὴν Ἰταλίαν ὁμόσε διδάξαντες, ἐμαρτύρησαν κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν καιρόν. Protulit hæc Eusebius lib. ii. Hist. c. 25.
thought_title: Peter and Paul's shared planting in Rome and Corinth
orientation: Dionysius is addressing the Roman church in a letter quoted by Eusebius, praising how Rome and Corinth have been joined through the teaching and martyrdom of Peter and Paul.
pass_a_gloss: These things you also, through such great admonition, have blended together the planting from Peter and Paul that came into being of Romans and of Corinthians. For indeed both, having planted us in our Corinth, taught in like manner. And in like manner, having taught together in Italy, they bore witness at the same time.

choices.why: The verb means to mix or blend together; it conveys the joining of the two churches through the shared apostolic planting.
The glossary requires 'planting' for φυτεία, used of the founding of churches by Peter and Paul.
The verb μαρτυρέω here means to bear witness by martyrdom; the literal sense 'bore witness' preserves the ambiguity and the source's wording.
The adverb means 'to the same place' or 'together'; it emphasizes that Peter and Paul taught jointly in Italy.
The phrase indicates simultaneity of their martyrdom, matching the brief's statement that they were martyred at the same time.

pass_b_english: "By this same admonition you too have blended together the planting of Romans and Corinthians that came into being from Peter and Paul. For both of them planted among us in our Corinth and taught us in like manner, and in like manner they taught together in Italy and bore witness at the same time."
notes: The source text includes a Latin editorial note: 'Protulit hæc Eusebius lib. ii. Hist. c. 25.' This is not part of the Greek text to translate. The first word Ταῦτα is marked with Valesius's emendation ταύτῃ; the gloss follows the transmitted reading Ταῦτα.
